introduction_markdown: Time allowed: two and a half hours. Answer ALL questions. Section I is designed to be answered in 1 hour and Section II in 1 1/2 hours; you are advised to divide your time accordingly. In Section II answer EITHER the a, b and c OR the d, e and f of each question. For your guidance the approximate mark for each part of a question is indicated in brackets. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Where necessary, assume: the acceleration of free fall, $g = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; the speed of light in air, $c = 3\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the charge on an electron, $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$. Calculators are allowed.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Define thermometric property. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Name the two fixed points used on the celsius scale for temperature measurements. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** A **thermometric property** is a physical property of a substance that **changes continuously and measurably with temperature**, so it can be used to measure temperature. Examples: the length of a mercury column in a glass tube, the resistance of a metal wire, the pressure of a fixed mass of gas at constant volume, the e.m.f. of a thermocouple.

**(ii)** The two fixed points of the Celsius scale are:

- the **lower fixed point (ice point)**: the temperature of pure melting ice, $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$;
- the **upper fixed point (steam point)**: the temperature of steam above water boiling at standard atmospheric pressure ($760\,\mathrm{mmHg}$), $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Define specific heat capacity. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Describe an experiment to measure the specific heat capacity of water. Your description should include:

- a diagram of the set-up
- the procedure you will use
- data or measurements
- how the data or measurements can be used to obtain the specific heat capacity
- any precaution taken

*[8 marks]*

(iii) Calculate the quantity of heat required to change the temperature of $2.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ of a liquid of specific heat capacity $4000\,\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ from $30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The **specific heat capacity** of a substance is the quantity of heat needed to raise the temperature of **$1\,\mathrm{kg}$** of the substance by **$1\,\mathrm{K}$** (or $1\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$). Its unit is $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.

**(ii)** I describe the **electrical method** (a heater of known power heats a known mass of water).

**1. Apparatus and diagram of the set-up**

Apparatus: a copper calorimeter with a lid and a stirrer; lagging (cotton wool or a felt jacket) around the calorimeter; an electric immersion heater (for example $12\,\mathrm{V}$, about $60\,\mathrm{W}$); a $12\,\mathrm{V}$ d.c. supply with a switch and a rheostat; an ammeter; a voltmeter; a thermometer ($0$ to $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$); a stopwatch; a top-pan balance; water.

Diagram (to be drawn): the calorimeter standing inside the lagging jacket and filled with water so that the heater is completely covered; the heater and the thermometer pass through holes in the lid, with the stirrer. Circuit: supply, switch, rheostat, ammeter and heater in **series**; the voltmeter connected **across the heater** (in parallel).

**2. Procedure**

1. Weigh the empty dry calorimeter ($m_1$). Put about $0.50\,\mathrm{kg}$ of water in it, enough to cover the heater, and weigh again ($m_2$). The mass of water is $m = m_2 - m_1$.
2. Assemble the set-up as in the diagram. Stir and read the initial temperature $\theta_1$.
3. Close the switch and **start the stopwatch at the same moment**. Adjust the rheostat to a convenient current and keep it constant; read the voltmeter $V$ and the ammeter $I$.
4. **Stir gently all the time.** After a time $t$ (for example $10$ minutes) open the switch and stop the stopwatch; keep stirring and record the **highest** temperature reached, $\theta_2$.

**3. Data or measurements**

Record: mass of water $m$; initial and final temperatures $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ (so the rise $\Delta\theta = \theta_2 - \theta_1$); voltage $V$; current $I$; time $t$. Illustrative readings: $m = 0.50\,\mathrm{kg}$, $V = 12\,\mathrm{V}$, $I = 5.0\,\mathrm{A}$, $t = 600\,\mathrm{s}$, $\Delta\theta = 17.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

**4. How the data are used to obtain the specific heat capacity**

The electrical energy supplied by the heater equals the heat gained by the water:

$$VIt = mc\,\Delta\theta \quad\Rightarrow\quad c = \frac{VIt}{m\,\Delta\theta}$$

With the illustrative readings: $c = \dfrac{12 \times 5.0 \times 600}{0.50 \times 17.5} = \dfrac{36000}{8.75} \approx 4.1 \times 10^{3}\,\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. (If the heat capacity of the calorimeter is taken into account, $VIt = (mc + m_{\mathrm{cal}}c_{\mathrm{cal}})\,\Delta\theta$.) The experiment can also be repeated for several times $t$ and a graph of $\theta$ against $t$ plotted: its slope equals $VI/(mc)$.

**5. Precautions**

- Lag the calorimeter and use a lid to reduce heat losses; it also helps to start a few degrees below room temperature and finish the same number of degrees above it.
- Stir continuously so that the temperature is uniform, and make sure the heater is fully immersed.
- Keep the current constant during heating; do not switch the heater on when it is out of the water.
- Keep the thermometer bulb in the water without touching the heater or the walls, and read it at eye level; record the highest temperature after switching off.

**(iii)**

$$Q = mc\,\Delta\theta$$

$m = 2.0\,\mathrm{kg}$, $c = 4000\,\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $\Delta\theta = 80 - 30 = 50\,^\circ\mathrm{C} = 50\,\mathrm{K}$.

$$Q = 2.0 \times 4000 \times 50 = 400\,000\,\mathrm{J} = 4.0\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{J}$$

**The heat required is $4.0\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{J}$** ($400\,\mathrm{kJ}$).

questions.enonce_markdown: Name the three methods by which heat can be transmitted from one place to another. *[3 marks]*

(i) Define a wave. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Name one wave which can travel through vacuum and another which cannot travel through vacuum. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** A **wave** is a disturbance (a vibration or oscillation) that **transfers energy from one place to another without transferring matter**.

**(ii)**

- A wave that can travel through a vacuum: **light** (any electromagnetic wave, for example radio waves or X-rays).
- A wave that cannot travel through a vacuum: **sound** (a mechanical wave, which needs a material medium; water waves are another example).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) State two factors which affect the speed of sound in air. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Describe an experiment to measure the speed of sound in air. Your description should include:

- a diagram of the set-up
- the procedure you will use
- data or measurements
- how the data or measurements can be used to obtain the speed of sound
- any precaution taken

*[8 marks]*

(iii) A stationary ship is $220\,\mathrm{m}$ from a high cliff. When it sounds its horn, an echo is heard $1.3$ seconds later. Calculate a value for the speed of sound in air. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Any two of: the **temperature** of the air (sound travels faster in warmer air); the **humidity** of the air (faster in moist air); the **wind** (the speed of the wind adds to or subtracts from the speed of sound).

**(ii)** I describe the **echo method**.

**1. Apparatus and diagram of the set-up**

Apparatus: a tall flat wall or cliff in an open field; a long measuring tape (or trundle wheel); a stopwatch; two wooden blocks (to make a sharp sound by clapping them together).

Diagram (to be drawn): the student standing at a distance $d$ in front of the wall with the two wooden blocks and the stopwatch; the arrow of the sound going to the wall and the arrow of the echo coming back; $d$ marked with a double arrow.

**2. Procedure**

1. Measure the distance $d$ from the student to the wall with the tape (for example about $85\,\mathrm{m}$).
2. Clap the blocks together once, then clap again each time the echo of the previous clap is heard, so that the claps keep time with the echoes.
3. Start the stopwatch on one clap (counted as zero) and count $n$ intervals (for example $n = 20$); stop it on the $n$th clap and read the total time $t$.
4. Repeat the measurement several times and take the mean time.

**3. Data or measurements**

Record the distance $d$, the number of intervals $n$ and the total time $t$ for each trial. Illustrative readings: $d = 85\,\mathrm{m}$, $n = 20$, $t = 10.0\,\mathrm{s}$.

**4. How the data are used to obtain the speed of sound**

The time between a clap and its echo is $t/n$. In this time the sound travels to the wall and back, a distance $2d$:

$$v = \frac{2d}{t/n} = \frac{2dn}{t}$$

With the illustrative readings: $v = \dfrac{2 \times 85 \times 20}{10.0} = 340\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

**5. Precautions**

- Stand far enough from the wall (at least $50\,\mathrm{m}$) so that the time interval is long enough to measure accurately.
- Count many echo intervals and average several trials, to reduce the error caused by the reaction time of the person with the stopwatch.
- Choose a calm day (little wind) and make sure no other wall or building gives a second echo; use a large, hard, flat reflecting surface.
- Measure the distance $d$ carefully (the tape straight and taut).

**(iii)** The sound goes to the cliff and back, so the total distance travelled is $2 \times 220 = 440\,\mathrm{m}$ in $1.3\,\mathrm{s}$:

$$v = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}} = \frac{2 \times 220\,\mathrm{m}}{1.3\,\mathrm{s}} = \frac{440}{1.3} = 338\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$$

**The speed of sound in air is about $338\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$** (about $340\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$).

questions.enonce_markdown: Name any three waves which form part of the electromagnetic spectrum. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown: Any three of: **radio waves, microwaves, infra-red, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays** (in order of increasing frequency).
